Perl is famous for its regular expressions (in short: regexes): this technology had been known for a long time, but Perl was probably the first general-purpose programming language to integrate them into the core. articles.author: Tend
articles.description:
Most productivity tools assume one thing.
That you already know what to do.
But in reality, that’s the hardest part.
*The Real Problem

Every day, we have thoughts like:
“I should start working out”
“I need to build this project”
“I should learn something new”
But turning that into:
clear tasks
priorities
a schedule
…takes effort.
So we either:
overthink it
delay it
or never start
*What I Wanted to Fix

I didn’t want another to-do app.
I wanted something that answers:
“What should I do next?”
Instead of managing tasks, I wanted a system that creates them for you.
The Idea
What if you could just type:
“I want to build a portfolio website”
And instantly get:
structured tasks
ordered steps
a plan for execution
That’s how Tend started.
*What Tend Does

Tend is an AI system that takes your thoughts and turns them into actionable plans.
You describe your goal.
It generates:
tasks
priorities
structure
direction
No manual breakdown needed.
Example
Input:
“I want to start a fitness routine”
Output:
Choose workout type
Set weekly schedule
Plan diet basics
Track progress
Instead of thinking, you start doing.
*Why This Matters

Most tools help you manage work.
Very few help you figure out the work itself.
That gap is where people get stuck.
Tend tries to remove that friction.
What I Learned Building This
A few interesting things:
People don’t struggle with discipline first
They struggle with clarity
The simpler the system, the more people use it
AI is most useful when it reduces thinking overhead
What’s Next
Right now, Tend is still evolving.
I’m exploring:
better task breakdown
smarter prioritization
deeper personalization
Try It
If this sounds interesting, you can check it out:
👉 https://maketend.com
*Would love to know:

Does this actually help?
Where does it fail?
What would make you use it daily?
articles.title: How I Built an AI That Turns Thoughts Into Actionable Plans

articles.author: Salvatore Attaguile
articles.description:
Hallucination isn’t an output problem.



  
  
  The Problem Isn’t Knowledge — It’s Control


Large language models don’t hallucinate because they “don’t know.”

They hallucinate because generation drifts.
At each step, the model predicts:

P(tokenₜ | context)
That context is constantly shifting.

Over time, something subtle happens:
The original prompt weakens

Recent tokens dominate

High-frequency patterns take over



This creates what can be described as semantic drift.
The model doesn’t suddenly “break.”

It gradually leaves the frame.
CAG introduces a simple constraint:
Every token must stay semantically aligned with a persistent frame.
Instead of letting generation run open-loop, we:
Create a semantic anchor from the prompt

Track how far each new token drifts

Intervene during de…
articles.title: Context-Anchored Generation (CAG): Fixing Hallucinations at the Decoding Layer

articles.author: Harm Rietmeijer
articles.description:
Most self-improvement apps track one thing — fitness, meditation, or money. But your life doesn't work in silos. You might be crushing it at the gym while your relationships suffer. Or earning great money but sleeping 5 hours a night.
COM-B Model — Understanding what drives behavior change
The AI doesn't just give generic advice. It calculates your score, identifies your weakest pillar, and suggests one micro-action you can attach to an existing habit. That's it. No 30-day challenge. No overwhelming dashboard. Just: here's your score, here's your lowest area, here's one thing to try this week.
People don't want more features — they want clarity.
Early versions had detailed breakdowns, charts, history graphs. Usage was low. When I simplified to just the score + one recommendation, engagement tripled.
The "gap" insight is the most valuable output.
Your overall score matters less than the gap between your highest and lowest pillar. A score of 7-7-7 is healthier than 9-9-3. People find this genuinely surprising.
Free works — but only with a clear value proposition.
"Free AI life coach" sounds like spam. "What's your Life Balance Score?" is a question people want to answer.
Open Source Framework
I've published the methodology as an open-source framework on GitHub: life-balance-framework
It includes:
The full self-assessment (15 questions across 3 pillars)
You can use it, adapt it, or contribute to it. MIT licensed.
Quick version: GitHub Pages calculator
I'd love to hear what your score is and whether the "weakest pillar" insight resonates. What would you build differently?
articles.title: How I Built a Free AI Life Coach That Real People Use

Java 26 Is Out — Here's What Actually Matters for Spring Boot Developers


Java 26 dropped today. And like every non-LTS release, most of the internet will spend the next week writing "everything new in Java 26" posts that include the Applet API removal and then act surprised you might care.
Let me skip straight to the three things that are actually relevant if you write Spring Boot applications for a living.
Ten JEPs, five final. No new language syntax reaches production-ready status. What you get is a faster runtime, HTTP/3 in the standard library, and the beginning of Java actually enforcing what final means.
